source.title: Open Problems in Hydrodynamical Approach to Relativistic Heavy Ion Collisions

accepted.question_text: How can hydrodynamical modeling of relativistic heavy-ion collisions be used to extract quantitative properties of quark-gluon plasma and the bulk QCD phase transition when very different model scenarios, including continuous emission, sudden freeze-out, final-state cascade calculations, and simplified blast-wave solutions, can reproduce the same observables after suitable parameter choices?
accepted.context_brief: Model degeneracy in hydrodynamic interpretation of QGP observables

evidence.quote: On the other hand, there exist several open problems in the interpretation of data in terms of the hydro model. These questions require careful examination to extract quantitative and precise information on the properties of QGP.

Furthermore, one should note that several very different physical scenarios within the hydrodynamical approach (e.g. the use of continuous emission, sudden freeze-out and rQMD final state cascade, or some drastically simplified hydro models such as blast wave solution, etc.) can give rise equally good results in reproducing the observables with suitable choices of parameters.

In order to extract more precise information on the properties of the quark-gluon plasma and the mechanism of phase transition in the bulk QCD matter, we should clarify these points and refine the physical parameters used in these approaches.

accepted.question_text: How can one determine whether the collective flow observed in relativistic heavy-ion collision data is genuinely hydrodynamic behavior based on local thermodynamical equilibrium, rather than a flow pattern produced by non-equilibrium dynamics that still obey local energy-momentum conservation or other force mechanisms?

evidence.quote: This is basically because the starting assumption of the validity of local thermodynamical equilibrium in hydrodynamics is not at all trivial to be justified for microscopic systems.
When we use the equation of state to describe the pressure as function of density, the hydrodynamical equations are meaningful only if the approximation of local thermal equilibrium is valid.
That is, a flow phenomena does not necessarily indicates the validity of the local thermodynamical equilibrium.

accepted.question_text: How can the initially produced QCD partonic excitations in a relativistic heavy-ion collision, which begin far from thermal equilibrium, reach a local-equilibrium quark-gluon plasma quickly enough to provide initial conditions compatible with successful hydrodynamical models, given that parton-cascade thermalization times with reasonable parton cross sections appear too long?

evidence.quote: At the first instant of the collision, these partonic degrees of freedom are far from thermal equilibrium. To obtain the initial condition suitable for the hydrodynamical scenario, we should understand how these partonic degrees of freedom reach the local equilibrium state, forming the quark-gluon plasma.

It seems that the time scale to achieve the thermal equilibrium in partonic cascade calculation within reasonable values of parton cross section is much larger than the time scale required for the hydrodynamical models. Thus the success of hydrodynamics cast a very interesting question of how such an early thermalization can be attained in the initially created QCD partonic excitations.
However, the isotropization itself is a necessary but not a sufficient condition for the thermal equilibrium.

accepted.question_text: How should event-by-event fluctuations in the non-smooth initial energy configuration of high-energy nuclear collisions be incorporated into hydrodynamical calculations so that event-averaged observables, especially the elliptic-flow coefficient v2 that measures azimuthal flow anisotropy, can be predicted quantitatively and used to recover information about the early collision state?

evidence.quote: The finite positive value of this coefficient v2 is referred to as the elliptic flow and, from the point of view of hydrodynamics, it is sensitive to the initial pressure gradient of the system.

Even the mechanism of thermalization is fast enough, the initial condition attained by high energy nuclear collision event is far from smooth as shown by the event generators such as NeXUS code. Furthermore, this initial configuration fluctuates collision by collision very largely, even for central collision of heavy nuclei.

Since the dynamical evolution of hydrodynamics is extremely non-linear, the event average of any hydrodynamical obserbable is quite different from the value calculated from the averaged smooth initial configuration, which is the hydrodynamcal calculations commonly used. The fluctuation of v2 coefficient must contain the dynamical information of the state formed in the early stage of the collision.

accepted.question_text: How can relativistic hydrodynamics for nuclear collisions be extended to include finite-size corrections when the microscopic mean-free path or correlation length λ_micro is not negligible compared with the hydrodynamical inhomogeneity scale λ_Hydro, so that the expansion parameter x = λ_micro/λ_Hydro is not much smaller than one, especially for determining local energy density and QCD phase-transition properties?

evidence.quote: Strictly speaking, the hydrodynamics is essentially the zero mean-free path (or correlation length) approximation for the microscopic degrees of freedom compared to the system size. For the nuclear collisions, this is not a trivial approximation.

The parameter which characterizes the degree of approximation with respect to the finite size of the system would be x = λmicro/λHydro where λmicro is the typical mean-free path (or the correlation length) of the constituent particles and λHydro is the hydrodynamical inhomogeneity scale.
Hydrodynamics is valid for x ≪ 1, so that when the local inhomogeneity scale in the system is of the order of the mean-free path, the hydrodynamics should break down.

In any case, the finite size effect on the local energy density is an important question, in particular with respect to the properties of phase transition. A further investigation on this direction is now in progress.

accepted.question_text: How can the viscosity of the quark-gluon plasma be analyzed quantitatively and consistently within relativistic hydrodynamics so that the apparently nearly ideal-fluid behavior observed at RHIC can be reconciled with dissipative effects, entropy-density arguments, and the conceptual and technical difficulties of relativistic dissipation?
accepted.context_brief: Quantitative viscosity effects in QGP hydrodynamics

evidence.quote: The comparison of flow phenomena to the ideal fluid calculation indicates that the emergence of new state of matter which flows like an ideal-fluid at RHIC energies.
On the other hand, Hirano and Gyulassy argue that this is due to the entropy density of the QGP which is much larger than the hadronic phase.

To be precise, a quantitative and consistent analysis of the viscosity within the framework of relativistic hydrodynamics has not yet been done completely. This is because the introduction of dissipative phenomena in relativistic hydrodynamics casts difficult problems, both conceptual and technical.
To extract more precise quantitative conclusion on the ideal nature of the QGP fluid, we should study the effect of dissipative processes on the collective flow variables.

accepted.question_text: How should final hadron spectra be constructed from hydrodynamical solutions of relativistic heavy-ion collisions when the standard Cooper-Frye sudden-freeze-out picture assumes emission from a sharp hypersurface but has conservation, negative-flux, and artificial-entropy-production problems, while continuous-emission models allow broad emission temperatures and can describe the same spectra and flow equally well?
accepted.context_brief: Freeze-out, continuous emission, and final hadron spectra

evidence.quote: To analyze the physical observables in terms of the hydrodynamical scenario, we have to construct the particle spectra from the hydro solution.
The Cooper-Frye formula gives the invariant momentum distribution in this case.

Although simple and elegant, this sudden freeze-out is not only an idealization but also contains some problems such as conservation of energy and momentum, negative flux and artificial entropy production.

It should be emphasized that the two extremely cases, a sharp temperature surface of sudden freeze-out and almost flat distribution of temperature of the continuous emission scenario give equally good description of the observed spectra and flow.

accepted.question_text: What practical covariant formulation of relativistic dissipative hydrodynamics can preserve causal signal propagation, avoid the acausal thermal-current behavior of the Landau formulation, and avoid the many unknown parameters, higher time derivatives, extra initial-condition difficulties, and numerical complications associated with the Israel-Stewart-Miller second-order theory?

evidence.quote: However, a covariant theory of dissipative phenomena is not trivial at all. We know that the diffusion equation is not covariant, and the equation is parabolic so that the propagation of signal has an infinite velocity.

However, this theory is too general and complex, containing many unknown parameters which make difficult the application of the theory to practical problems. Furthermore, the theory contains the third order time derivatives, introducing additional difficulties of initial value problem and numerical procedure.
Because of the simple form of viscous terms, incorporation of these equations to the realistic hydro-code such as SPHERIO is relatively easy. A work on this line is in progress.

accepted.question_text: Which observables can serve as signals of genuine hydrodynamic behavior in relativistic heavy-ion collisions, beyond successful fits by hydrodynamical models, and how can candidates such as shock-wave propagation be identified in order to reduce the remaining conceptual and quantitative uncertainties?

evidence.quote: However, from the quantitative point of view, the present hydrodynamical approach still contains many uncertainties and also some conceptual problems.

Other questions as early thermalization, finite size effects, fluctuations in initial conditions, etc. should also be studied more in detail When these questions are clarified, we will have much more detailed knowledge about the dynamics and properties of the new states of strongly interacting matter.
It is also quite important to look for signals of genuine hydrodynamics, such as shock wave propagation.
